general_information.Description: Economics is the study of how society manages its scarce resources. Economics has been divided into the subcategories of microeconomics and macroeconomics. While microeconomics focuses on the behavior of individual economic agents, this course - macroeconomics - studies how economists measure macroeconomic variables and covers topics such as determination of national output, economic growth, unemployment, inflation, interest rates, and exchange rates. Macroeconomics also discusses and assesses the effectiveness of monetary and fiscal policies under different scenarios.
general_information.StudentTasks: + Class attendance is strongly encouraged. Attend at least 80% of class hours in order to be accepted to the final examination + Read textbooks and other materials in advance before the class + Actively participate in class activities + Complete all homework assignments and other tasks given by the instructor + Use personal laptop in class only for learning purposes + Don’t have private conversations or arrive at class late, which can disrupt the learning environment of the class

learning_outcomes.CLO Details: Discuss the theory of supply and demand
Recognize the influences of market equilibrium and disequilibrium
Describe the theory of supply and demand in real-life scenarios
Identify the tools and strategies to understand supply and demand applications
Apply CPI and GDP to prices and unemployment
Review the influences of aggregate demand and aggregate supply
Shows self-reliance when working independently and collaboratively
Demonstrate ethical awareness and reflection in business context

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: GDP is defined as the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period of time. In spite of this definition, some production is left out of GDP. Ex-plain why some final goods and services are not included.

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Explain why it is the case that the value of intermediate goods produced and sold during the year is not included directly as part of GDP, but the value of intermediate goods produced and not sold is included directly as part of GDP.

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Since it is counted as investment, why doesn't the purchase of earthmoving equipment from China by a U.S. corporation increase U.S. GDP?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: You find that your paycheck for the year is higher this year than last. Does that mean that your real income has increased? Explain carefully.

constructive_questions.Name: DN3
constructive_questions.Details: U.S. real GDP is substantially higher today than it was 60 years ago. What does this tell us, and what does it not tell us, about the well-being of U.S. residents?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Which is likely to have the larger effect on the CPI, a 2 percent increase in the price of food or a 3 percent in-crease in the price of diamond rings? Explain.

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: List the three major problems in using the CPI as a measure of the cost of living.

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Why does the GDP deflator give a different rate of inflation than the CPI?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: linda and Kevin meet George, the banker, to work out the details of a mortgage. They all expect that infla-tion will be 2 percent over the term of the loan, and they agree on a nominal interest rate of 6 percent. As it turns out, the inflation rate is 5 percent over the term of the loan. a. What was the expected real interest rate? b. What was the actual real interest rate? c. Who benefited and who lost because of the unexpected inflation?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: In a simple economy, people consume only 2 goods, food and clothing. The market basket of goods used to compute the CPI consists of 50 units of food and 10 units of clothing. Food Clothing 2002 price per unit $4 $10 2003 price per unit $6 $20 Do these price changes affect all consumers to the same extent? Explain.

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Following the recession of 2001, there was a month in which employment and the unemploy-ment rate both rose. Assuming the computations were correct, how is it possible for both to have increased?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Why have labor-force participation rates for women in the United States increased since World War II while labor-force participation rates for men have decreased?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Most spells of unemployment are short, and most unemployment observed at any given time is long term. How can this be?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Why might a favorable change in the economy, such as technological improvement or a de-crease in the price of imported oil, be associated with an increase in frictional unemployment?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Teenage unemployment is higher than unemployment of people ages 20 and over. Explain why economists would attribute at least part of this difference to minimum-wage laws.

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Why is productivity related to the standard of living? In your answer be sure to explain what productivity and standard of living mean. Make a list of things that determine labor productiv-ity.

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: What is a production function? Write an equation for a typical production function, and ex-plain what each of the terms represents.

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: What is the difference between human capital and technology?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: The catch-up effect says that countries with low income can grow faster than countries with higher income. However, in statistical studies that include many diverse countries we do not observe the catch-up-effect unless we control for other variables that affect productivity. Con-sidering the determinants of productivity, list and explain some things that would tend to pro-hibit or limit a poor country's ability to catch up with the rich ones.

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: In addition to investment in physical and human capital, what other public policies might a country adopt to increase productivity?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: What are the basic differences between bonds and stocks?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Which of the two bonds in each example would you expect to generally pay the higher interest rate? Explain why.

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose that you are a broker and people tell you the following about themselves. What sort of bond would you recommend to each? Defend your choices.

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: In the national income accounting identity showing the equality between national saving and investment, what are the algebraic expressions for private saving and public saving?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Explain why the demand for loanable funds slopes downward and why the supply of loanable funds slopes upward.

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Economists argue that the move from barter to money increased trade and production. How is this possible?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Are credit cards and debit cards money? What's the difference between credit and debit cards?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: What is the difference between commodity money and fiat money? Why do people accept fiat money in trade for goods and services?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: What does the text mean by the question, "Where Is All the Currency?" How does it answer the question?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: What is meant by the term "lender of last resort?" In what circumstances might the Fed be a lender of last resort?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Explain the adjustment process in the money market that creates a change in the price level when the money supply increases.

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose the Fed sells government bonds. Use a graph of the money market to show what this does to the value of money.

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Using separate graphs, demonstrate what happens to the money supply, money demand, the value of money, and the price level if MS increases?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: According to the classical dichotomy, what changes nominal variables? What changes real variables?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Wages and prices are many times higher today than they were 30 years ago, yet people do not work a lot more hours or buy fewer goods. How can this be?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: What is the inflation tax, and how might it explain the creation of inflation by a central bank?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Economists agree that increases in the money-supply growth rate increase inflation and that inflation is undesirable. So why have there been hyperinflations and how have they been ended?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Inflation distorts relative prices. What does this mean and why does it impose a cost on society?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Explain the difference between absolute advantage and comparative advantage. Which is more important in determining trade patterns, absolute advantage or comparative advantage? Why?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Julia can fix a meal in 1 hour, and her opportunity cost of one hour is $50. Jacque can fix the same kind of meal in 2 hours, and his opportunity cost of one hour is $20. Will both Julia and Jacque be better off if she pays him $45 per meal to fix her meals? Explain.

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Mike and Sandy are two woodworkers who both make tables and chairs. In one month, Mike can make 4 tables or 20 chairs, where Sandy can make 6 tables or 18 chairs. Given this, we know that the opportunity cost of 1 chair is

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose that Bill, a resident of the U.S., buys software from a company in Japan. Explain why and in what directions this changes U.S. net exports and U.S. net capital outflow.

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Why are net exports and net capital outflow always equal?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Colonial America had little industry and so had mostly raw materials to export. At the same time, there were many opportunities to purchase capital goods and earn a high rate of return because there was little existing capital so that the marginal product of capital was relatively high. What does this suggest about net exports and net capital outflow in colonial America?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose that a country has $120 billion of national saving, and $80 billion of domestic investment. Is this possible? Where did the other $40 billion of national savings go?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: How do the nominal exchange rate and the real exchange rate differ?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: How do we find the real exchange rate from the nominal exchange rate?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose a bottle of wine costs 25 euros in France and 20 dollars in the United States. If the exchange rate is 1.25 euros per dollar, what is the real exchange rate?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: What is the logic behind the theory of purchasing-power parity?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose that a U.S. dollar buys more gold in Australia than it buys in Russia. What does purchasing-power parity imply should happen?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: What does purchasing-power parity imply about the real exchange rate?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: According to purchasing-power parity, what is the relationship between changes in price levels between two countries and changes in nominal exchange rates?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Can purchasing-power parity be used to explain the fact that the U.S. dollar has depreciated by more than 50 percent against the German mark between 1970 and 1998, but appreciated by more than 100 percent against the Italian lira during the same period? Defend your answer.

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose that money supply growth continues to be higher in Turkey than it is in the United States. What does purchasing-power parity imply will happen to the real and to the nominal exchange rate?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Under what circumstances does purchasing-power parity explain how exchange rates are determined, and why is it not completely accurate?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose a lobster supper in Maine costs fewer dollars than a Lobster supper in Paris, France. Explain why this is inconsistent with purchasing-power parity and explain why the inconsistency may exist.

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose that U.S. investors decide that investment opportunities in African countries have improved. What happens to U.S. net capital outflow? What happens to the U.S. real interest rate?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Explain how the relation between the real exchange rate and net exports explains the downward slope of the demand for foreign-currency exchange curve.

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: How are the identities S = NCO + I and NCO = NX related to the foreign currency exchange market and the loanable funds market?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Explain how an increase in the demand for capital goods in the U.S. can lead to a change in the U.S. exchange rate.

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose that U.S. citizens start saving more. What does this imply about the supply of loanable funds and the equilibrium real interest rate? What happens to the real exchange rate?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose that the Turkish government budget deficit increases. What curves in the open-economy macroeconomic model shift? Explain why each curve shifts the direction it does.

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose a presidential candidate promises to increase the government budget surplus and claims that doing so will stop U.S. citizens from investing in foreign companies and increase the value of the dollar. Evaluate this promise.

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: What effect do protectionist policies have on the trade deficit?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose the U.S. government institutes a "Buy American" campaign, in order to encourage spending on domestic goods. What effect will this have on the U.S. trade balance?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: What do trade policies do to the standard of living?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: If a county becomes more likely to default on its bonds, what happens to that country’s interest rate and exchange rate? Explain

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: What variables besides real GDP tend to decline during recessions? Given the definition of real GDP, argue that declines in these variables are to be expected.

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: What do most economists believe concerning the relation between the price level and real output?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Explain how an increase in the price level changes interest rates. How does this change in interest rates lead to changes in investment and net exports?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Use sticky-wage theory to explain why an increase in the expected price level shifts the aggregate supply curve.

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: Suppose that a decrease in the demand for goods and services pushes the economy into recession. What happens to the price level? If the government does nothing, what ensures that the economy still eventually gets back to the natural rate of output?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: What is the difference between monetary policy and fiscal policy?

constructive_questions.Name: DN2
constructive_questions.Details: There are three factors that help explain the slope of the aggregate demand curve. Which two are less important? Why are they less important?

constructive_questions.Name: DN1
constructive_questions.Details: Explain why the interest rate is the opportunity cost of holding currency. What is the benefit of holding currency?
